title: “BE HOLY AS I AM HOLY” WAS NEVER A SUGGESTION
paragraphs:
“BE HOLY AS I AM HOLY” WAS NEVER A SUGGESTION
We have become dangerously comfortable asking Jesus to forgive the very sins we have quietly decided we will never surrender.
There is a version of Christianity that almost everyone can tolerate.
Go to church when life permits.
Ask God to bless the relationship, the ambition, the business, the plans.
Say, “Nobody is perfect” whenever conviction becomes uncomfortable.
And continue living almost exactly as before.
It is Christianity with forgiveness but no transformation.
A Savior who rescues but supposedly has no authority to rule.
A cross that removes guilt but never crucifies the old life.
And then Peter walks into our comfortable religion carrying words sharp enough to tear the disguise from our hearts:
Be holy if that fits your personality.
Be holy once your circumstances improve.
Be holy when temptation becomes easier.
Be holy unless everyone around you thinks holiness is outdated.
God does not present holiness as an optional upgrade for unusually serious Christians.
He calls His people to it.

And perhaps the reason those words disturb us is that somewhere along the way many of us began treating Jesus as Someone who came merely to make us feel better about the person we refuse to stop being.
But Jesus did not die merely to make sinning more comfortable.
And salvation is far more glorious than permission to remain chained to what was destroying us.
That old English word “conversation” does not merely mean the words coming out of your mouth. The underlying Greek speaks about your manner of life—your conduct.
The Greek of 1 Peter 1:15 contains a devastating little phrase:
Not conduct when somebody from church is watching.
The secret habit you have renamed “my struggle” because calling it sin would require you to confront it.
The way you treat your spouse.
The way you speak when angry.
The way you behave when lonely.
The person you become when nobody who admires you is in the room.
Peter gives Christianity nowhere to hide.
But there is something even more important here.
Peter did not invent this command.
He reaches backward into Israel's Scriptures, where God told His covenant people:
“You shall be holy, for I am holy.”

The Hebrew word qadosh carries the idea of holiness, sacredness, being set apart. God is utterly holy, and the people who belong to Him are therefore summoned into a life that reflects the character of the One to whom they belong.
“Be holy because holiness produces better results.”
“Be holy because religious people should behave themselves.”
Christian holiness is not fundamentally about constructing an impressive spiritual reputation.
And the terrifying beauty of grace is that Jesus loves us far too deeply to rescue us from sin's condemnation while leaving us peacefully surrendered to sin's domination.
Maybe that is where this becomes painfully personal.
Because some of us know exactly where the locked room is.
but there is one door we keep asking Him not to open.
One corner of the heart where we have quietly hung a sign:
You can talk about grace beautifully.
when there is nobody left to impress...
But it should also become one of the most comforting sentences you have ever heard.
Not the person everybody thinks you are.
He knows what you keep remembering.
He knows what you desperately hope nobody discovers.
He knows the thing that makes you wonder whether you have gone too far.
And this is where Christianity becomes unlike every self-improvement religion human beings could invent.
Because the holy God who exposes sin is also the God who came looking for sinners.
Jesus Christ did not stand at a safe distance from our corruption shouting instructions about how we could climb our way toward Him.
He called adulterers away from sin.
He walked toward a cross carrying sins He never committed.
This is why holiness must never be preached apart from the Gospel.
Otherwise holiness becomes either pride or despair.
At the cross, nobody gets to boast.
And nobody who comes to Christ in repentance has to believe redemption is impossible.
The ground beneath Calvary is level.
We bring a debt we cannot pay.
He brings blood sufficient to redeem.
Peter himself anchors this call to holiness in redemption, telling believers that they were not redeemed with corruptible things such as silver and gold, but with the precious blood of Christ.
That means holiness is not the entrance fee for salvation.
Holiness is the life of a person who has been purchased by Someone infinitely precious.
You do not become holy enough so that Jesus will finally decide to save you.
You run to Jesus because you cannot save yourself.
And the Jesus who saves you begins transforming you.
Grace is not God's permission to remain enslaved.
Grace is God's power and mercy meeting people who could never free themselves.
Repentance is not merely feeling terrible after sin.
You can hate consequences without hating sin.
You can cry because you were caught.
You can apologize because your marriage is collapsing.
You can promise God everything because you are frightened.
And after the crisis disappears, you can walk straight back toward the same chains.
It stops negotiating with the darkness.
“How close can I get to sin without technically crossing the line?”
“How completely can my life belong to Christ?”
One heart wants boundaries because it wants to keep as much sin as Christianity will permit.
Maybe you have spent years asking the wrong question.
“Does this make me more like Jesus?”
Because holiness is not merely avoiding a list of forbidden behaviors.
He is not merely our example; He is our Savior, Lord, righteousness, hope and life.
And transformation into Christlikeness reaches places religious performance never touches.
Holiness means telling the truth when lying would protect you.
Fleeing sexual immorality when your body screams for compromise.
Refusing pornography when nobody would discover it.
Returning money that does not belong to you.
Putting the bottle down when it has become your master.
Refusing gossip even when the story is irresistible.
Choosing integrity when compromise would make you richer.
Saying, “Jesus, this belongs to You too.”
That is where holiness becomes costly.
And that is precisely where many people discover whether they wanted Jesus...
or merely wanted relief from hell.
There is a Christianity that asks:
And there is discipleship that eventually falls trembling before Him and asks:
“Lord, what have I withheld from You?”
Perhaps you already know the answer.
And perhaps while reading this, one particular thing has been coming repeatedly into your mind.
Do not immediately push it away.
Because Christ has already opened the door of mercy for sinners who come to Him.
There is no holiness without grace.
But there is also no biblical grace that teaches us to make peace with rebellion against God.
The same Peter who commands holiness begins this section by pointing believers toward grace.
He tells them to set their hope fully on the grace coming through Jesus Christ.
Grace and holiness are not enemies.
Grace is why holiness is possible without becoming hopeless.
run toward Christ rather than away from Him.
This is important because somebody reading this has confused holiness with sinless perfection.
You failed again, and now you think God must be finished with you.
This is the man who swore that even if everyone else abandoned Jesus, he would remain.
Imagine the silence after the rooster crowed.
Imagine realizing that the voice you had just used to deny knowing Jesus was the same voice that once declared Him the Christ.
Peter knew what it felt like to discover that your courage was weaker than you thought.
Yet Peter's story did not end beside that charcoal fire of denial.
The risen Jesus came for him.
And eventually this once-broken disciple wrote to other believers:
The command came through a restored failure.
Which means holiness is not the testimony of people who never fell.
It is the calling of people whom grace refuses to leave on the ground.
Not by pretending the scandal never happened.
Not by renaming darkness as light.
Not by lowering God's holiness until our rebellion becomes acceptable.
The cross tells the truth about how serious sin is and, at exactly the same time, reveals how astonishing God's mercy is.
If sin were trivial, Calvary would make no sense.
But if your sin were beyond God's ability to redeem, Calvary would offer no hope.
At the cross both lies die.
Sin is worse than we wanted to admit.
Grace is greater than we dared to believe.
You do not have to polish the chains before bringing them to Jesus.
Bring the thing you cannot believe you did.
Bring the thing you keep doing.
Bring the heart that is tired of promising God, “Never again,” only to return three days later.
Jesus receives sinners as they come...
and then calls them to follow Him.
You cannot clutch your chains and simultaneously complain that Christ refuses to free your hands.
There comes a moment when grace calls you to surrender.
Maybe your prayer needs to become brutally simple:

“Lord Jesus Christ, I have called You Savior while resisting You as Lord. Forgive me. Expose whatever I have protected from You. I cannot cleanse myself. I cannot save myself. I trust Your finished work, Your death and resurrection. Give me strength to turn from sin. Teach me to hate what destroys communion with You and love what pleases You. Make my private life belong to You. Make my public life belong to You. Make all of me Yours. Amen.”
And if that prayer exposed something hidden, do not turn this moment into another emotional experience you forget tomorrow.
Ask forgiveness where forgiveness needs to be asked.
Find mature Christian accountability where secrecy has been feeding sin.
Get connected to a faithful local church.
but because you belong to the One who saved you.
Not because typing those words saves you.
But perhaps someone else hiding behind a screen needs to discover that they are not the only believer fighting a war nobody sees.
And if Christ has already been restoring something in you that once seemed impossible to redeem, tell us.
Your testimony might become somebody else's reason not to give up tonight.
Not because sharing a Facebook post earns God's favor. It does not.

But if this truth glorifies Christ, helps awaken sleeping believers, reaches somebody trapped in secret sin, or puts the Gospel in front of a person who would never walk through a church door, then sharing it can become a simple act of witness.
Send it to the friend whose faith has grown cold.
Send it to the Christian who needs courage.
Send it even to the person who does not yet believe.
There may come a night when temptation returns and you need to remember that holiness is not God trying to steal your joy.
It is the Holy One calling you away from the things that have been stealing you.
Supporting Gospel ministry does not purchase God's favor.

But Christians can freely support work they believe is faithfully spreading biblical truth, and your support can help Gospel Warrior keep creating, publishing and sharing resources designed to point people toward Jesus Christ.
He is the One who shed His blood.
He is the One who rose.
He is the One who forgives repentant sinners.
He is the One who transforms lives.
He is the One worthy of your obedience.
do not hear the voice of a cruel God demanding that wounded people climb an impossible mountain alone.
Hear the voice of the Holy One who redeemed His people and calls them to become what His grace is transforming them to be.
You will discover weaknesses you did not know existed.
There may be relationships you have to leave.
There may be habits you have to starve.
There may be doors you must permanently close.
There may be moments when obedience costs far more than compromise would have cost.
Holiness is not optional because Jesus is not merely an accessory attached to your old life.
And perhaps the greatest tragedy would not be discovering that following Christ costs you something.
Perhaps the greatest tragedy would be spending your entire life protecting the very chains from which Jesus died to set you free.
So bring Him the locked room.
Bring Him the version of yourself nobody else has met.
Then watch what grace does with a life that finally stops hiding.
Because one surrendered life can become another person's evidence that Jesus still restores sinners.
And remember this when the shame comes whispering your old name:
The scandal may explain where you have been—but only Jesus gets to write where redemption takes you next.
